facts.fact: December 1942: Béatrice has only the horses left for comfort; every morning she and her daughter Fanny retreat to the Bois de Boulogne, where she can ignore what waits outside the park gates; she makes no move to leave — she should have gone long ago, but routine holds her, and the July Vel d’Hiv roundup of Jews has already happened.
facts.quote: BY DECEMBER 1942, BÉATRICE had only the horses for comfort. In the mornings, she and her daughter Fanny retreated to the Bois de Boulogne, the garden Napoleon III gave to the city in 1852, a manicured wilderness where society women like Béatrice could ride and learn to endure. In those hours, she could ignore what awaited her outside the park gates. She should have left long ago, but routine held her. In July, the Vel d’Hiv roundup of Jews had happened.

facts.fact: On the afternoon of December 5 Béatrice and Fanny are stopped: no struggle, just uniforms and the demand for identity papers; they hand the papers over, it doesn't matter; they are arrested and their names logged after midnight at the police station in the 16th arrondissement in the Consignes Provisoires ledger. No charge is listed, but the word spreads in the family that they had not been wearing gold stars.
facts.quote: On the afternoon of December 5, Béatrice and Fanny were stopped. There was no struggle, just uniforms, and the demand for identity papers. They gave them, but it didn’t matter. They were arrested and their names logged after midnight at the police station in the 16th arrondissement in the Consignes Provisoires ledger, that bleak manuscript of erasure in curls of handwriting. There was no charge listed, but the word spread in their family that they had not been wearing gold stars.

facts.fact: The entire police record of both women is one word written in the columns beside their names: Juive — the label that gives the chapter its title.
facts.quote: In the ledger, there was just one word in the columns by their names: Juive.

facts.fact: Irène Anspach, Béatrice's paternal cousin, is standing beside them at the arrest and, though also Jewish, is left untouched; Béatrice makes one hurried decision — she slips Irène her gold identity bracelet, a gourmette — and Irène then goes inside to gather what she can, among them the 1923 Georges Malissard sculpture of Béatrice on horseback; Irène's family keeps it for twenty-five years and donates it to the Camondo museum in 1967.
facts.quote: Béatrice slipped her a gold identity bracelet, a gourmette, in that kind of hurried gesture you make when you know the rest is already gone. And then Irène Anspach went inside, apparently to gather what she could. Perhaps a scrapbook. A 1923 Georges Malissard sculpture: Béatrice on horseback, side-saddle, with a riding crop in her hand. For twenty-five years Irène Anspach and her family kept it, a monument to the passion Béatrice loved. Her family donated it to the Camondo museum in 1967.

facts.fact: The Neuilly building was already targeted before the arrest: in 1940 Léon and eight other Jewish residents were forced off the building's management group and an administrateur proviseur appointed; by 1942 almost all those owners had fled, subletting or letting the Germans seize their flats, and only Béatrice and Fanny remain — they stay as if staying might postpone what was already coming.
facts.quote: In 1940, Léon and eight other Jewish residents were forced off the building’s management group and an administrateur proviseur was appointed for the property. By 1942, almost all of those Jewish owners had fled the building, forced to either sublet their apartments or let their flats be seized by the Germans. Only Béatrice and Fanny remained. There is something tragic in their endurance, something almost noble, though no one at the time would have said so aloud. They stayed as if it might postpone what was already coming.

facts.fact: Mayor Edmond Bloud, already replaced for being too lenient with Jews, balks at removing Jewish municipal employees, resists denunciations and property seizures, quietly delays exclusion orders and keeps helping Jewish residents with paperwork — discretion that amounts to defiance — until Vichy's prefect dismisses him, citing “failure to apply measures of national renewal”; l’Action Française calls him “A Bad Frenchman”, and in January 1942 Vichy installs Max Roger, after whom police raids, property seizures and the Devisenschutzkommando operate a short walk from Béatrice's home.
facts.quote: He balked at removing Jewish municipal employees, resisted denunciations and property seizures, quietly delayed exclusion orders, and continued to help Jewish residents with paperwork when such help was already dangerous. In the tightening political atmosphere, this discretion amounted to defiance. Vichy’s prefect dismissed him, citing “failure to apply measures of national renewal”—a bureaucratic euphemism for refusing to enforce antisemitic laws.

facts.fact: Rudi de Mérode (born Frédéric Martin, self-styled “the prince”, holding court at number 70 Boulevard Maurice-Barrès) leads the Gestapo de Neuilly: his gang loots the apartments of Jews, tortures victims in basements, lives on silence and fear with 30 percent commissions, forces Jewish owners to buy back their own gold and jewelry at bargain prices — and deports those who refuse; after the war the Interior Ministry tallies his fortune at nearly 1 billion francs (about $94 million today) and the gang figures in the deportations of more than five hundred people; when the war turns he slips to Madrid as the “Prince de Mérode” and is believed to have died after 1970.
facts.quote: Rudi and his gang looted the apartments of Jews. They tortured their victims in basements. They made their money from silence and fear—30 percent commissions on the value of whatever they took. After the war, the Interior Ministry tallied up Mérode’s fortune: nearly 1 billion francs, about $94 million today. Cash, jewels, gold—bundled in cupboards, buried in gardens. They had the power to open up private bank vaults and buy jewelry and bars of gold back from the Jewish owners at bargain prices. If they refused, they were deported. And the Gestapo de Neuilly figured in the deportations of more than five hundred people. That was the real profit.

facts.fact: On the eve of her arrest Béatrice manages to send a note to her cousin Irène saying everything is fine; within days trucks arrive and are parked just long enough to empty her home — two apartments of antique furniture and heirlooms, three Pleyel pianos, a Louis XVI bronze pendulum clock signed “Leroy haut OM18,” the portrait of Léon's father Théodore — after which the Commissariat-General for Jewish Affairs documents the erasure as accounting (seizure of 14,933 shares, apartment sealed) and Léon's music, the Kérylos archive, drawings, plans, letters and four thousand leather-bound books vanish.
facts.quote: On the eve of her arrest, Béatrice managed to send a note to her cousin Irène, telling her everything was fine, according to relatives decades later. But the occupiers moved quickly. Within days the trucks came. They parked just long enough to empty her home—two apartments, spread lavishly with antique furniture and family heirlooms.

relationships.relationship: Béatrice — Fanny: mother and daughter; they retreat to the park together every morning and are stopped, arrested and logged together on December 5.
relationships.quote: she and her daughter Fanny retreated to the Bois de Boulogne

relationships.relationship: Béatrice — Irène Anspach: paternal cousins; Irène is present at the arrest, is not arrested, receives Béatrice's gold gourmette and the 1923 Malissard equestrian statue, and the note of reassurance sent on the eve of the arrest; her family donates the statue in 1967.
relationships.quote: Irène Anspach, Béatrice’s paternal cousin, had stood beside them when they were arrested.

relationships.relationship: Sophie Le Tarnec — the Camondo museum / Irène Anspach: archivist of forty years there; she records that Irène was present at the arrest and gave the statue to the museum, and is still mystified how Irène came to hold it and why she was not arrested; the archives give no clarity on whether Béatrice and Fanny were denounced.
relationships.quote: “Irène Anspach was present at the arrest of Béatrice and Fanny. And it was, in fact, Irène Anspach who gave Béatrice’s equestrian statue to the museum, in her memory. How did she come to have it in her possession? I could not tell you. Likewise, why was she not arrested as well?”

relationships.relationship: Béatrice and Fanny — Léon: Léon is named as one of the Jewish owners pushed off the building's management group in 1940, and his music is among the seized papers; the text of this chapter never states his relationship to Béatrice.
relationships.quote: In 1940, Léon and eight other Jewish residents were forced off the building’s management group

relationships.relationship: Léon — Théodore: father and son; Théodore's portrait was painted at Villa Kérylos, the home he built to remember a civilization and gave to the French state.
relationships.quote: Léon’s father, Théodore, painted at Villa Kérylos, the home he had built to remember a civilization, his gift to the French state.

relationships.relationship: Edmond Bloud — Max Roger: successive mayors of Neuilly; Bloud, also the editor of a Catholic publishing house, is dismissed for leniency toward Jews and replaced in January 1942 by Roger, “a colorless industrial perfume chemist” under whom raids and seizures follow.
relationships.quote: Max Roger, a colorless industrial perfume chemist, understood what was expected of him.

relationships.relationship: Rudi de Mérode — the Gestapo de Neuilly and the Germans: born Frédéric Martin, calls himself “the prince”, leads a French paramilitary gang of some one or two dozen gestapistes français and profiteers from number 70 Boulevard Maurice-Barrès, working hand in hand with Gestapo and SS authorities — doing what the Germans preferred not to be seen doing — a short walk from Béatrice's home.
relationships.quote: led the Gestapo de Neuilly, a French paramilitary gang that worked hand in hand with the Germans, doing the things the Germans preferred not to be seen doing.

relationships.relationship: Neuilly-sur-Seine — the Occupation: a wealthy commune across the Seine from the Arc de Triomphe with a substantial Jewish population, outwardly calm, “a geography where people vanished into police files, boardinghouses, checkpoints, and the machinery of the Occupation”.
relationships.quote: a geography where people vanished into police files, boardinghouses, checkpoints, and the machinery of the Occupation
